records.name_note: Left null due to a genuine spelling conflict between admissible sources' own structured taxonomy fields, not resolved by either source. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page is titled "Atropa bella-donna (Belladonna, Deadly Nightshade)" and its structured Attributes block reads "Genus: Atropa Species: bella-donna Family: Solanaceae" -- the hyphenated epithet. RHS's page, by contrast, is titled "Atropa belladonna | deadly nightshade" (no hyphen) and its Botanical Details block carries an explicit "Name Status Correct" determination anchored to that taxon record (RHS's page-level structured Taxon data gives the species name as "Atropa belladonna"). Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder also uses the unhyphenated "Atropa belladonna" throughout its Noteworthy Characteristics prose. No admissible source acknowledges or reconciles the other spelling, so no single accepted binomial can be asserted without picking a side.
records.toxicity_detail: All three admissible sources that cover this species agree it is a high-severity, whole-plant toxic species (tropane alkaloids as the toxic principle) and that the risk extends specifically to cats and dogs, not just to humans. RHS's structured "Potentially harmful" fields state: "TOXIC if eaten; avoid eye contact. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and, in a separately scoped line naming the animals, "Pets (dogs, cats): TOXIC if eaten; avoid eye contact." Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder states in prose: "The foliage, fruits and roots of this plant are extremely toxic, containing tropane alkaloids such as atropine, scopolamine and hyoscyamine. In humans, small doses of material from this plant will produce delirium and hallucinations, but larger doses will kill. ... Consumption of as few as two berries can kill a child. Consumption of 10 berries is often lethal to an adult. Dogs and cats are susceptible to the poison, but many other animals and birds can eat the fruits with no ill effects." NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists "Problem for Cats" and "Problem for Dogs" (alongside Problem for Horses, Problem for Children, and Poisonous to Humans) among its structured Problems tags, and its Poison Symptoms field reads: "Highly toxic. Small doses will produce delirium and hallucinations, larger doses will kill. Fever, rapid pulse, dilation of pupils, hot and dry flushed skin, headache, dry mouth, difficulty of swallowing, burning of the throat, hallucinations, convulsions. May cause death in livestock and pets," naming the Poison Toxic Principle as "Tropane alkaloids, atropine, and others" and the Poison Part as "Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems." NC State's general Description (not confined to its human-specific poison block) adds: "The plant is so toxic that if an open wound comes in contact with the leaves, roots or fruits, the results can be fatal. Domestic pets can also suffer the effects of this toxic plant." No admissible source disputes toxicity to pets or to humans.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension rates this species' poison severity "High" and gives Poison Symptoms as "Highly toxic, may be fatal if eaten. Nausea, vomiting, salivation, drowsiness, abdominal pain, low blood pressure, low heart rate, diarrhea, dilated pupils, weakness, respiratory depression; may be fatal to humans, pets, and livestock," with Poison Toxic Principle "Solanine and other alkaloids" present in the Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, and Stems (essentially the whole plant). That symptom text sits nested under NC State's "Poisonous to Humans:" section header, but its own prose explicitly extends to "pets," and this is corroborated by two independently structured, pet-specific claims: NC State's separate Problems list names "Problem for Cats" and "Problem for Dogs" specifically (alongside "Poisonous to Humans," "Problem for Children," and "Problem for Horses"), and RHS's toxicity box states "Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten." Cats and dogs are each named by at least one source, satisfying this catalog's toxic_to_pets scope.

RHS gives only a categorical hardiness rating (H5: hardy in most UK locations even in severe winters, roughly -15 to -10°C) and NC State gives only USDA zone-level winter-hardiness (Zones 3a-8b) -- these are survival/hardiness-zone statements, not a specific damage-onset figure, so were not mapped onto this field.

NC State's structured Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) as separate unranked category tags, and RHS's own cultivation guidance states soil 'doesn't matter whether your soil is acidic or alkaline, as long as the ground is moist but well-drained' -- explicitly disclaiming a pH requirement. water_dormant_days_est, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm: no admissible source gives a winter/dormant-season watering frequency, a soil dry-down target, or a moisture-check depth for this deciduous shrub.

water_regime keep_moist is a judgment call, not a verbatim match: it is inferred from three species-specific sources that each gesture toward maintaining adequate moisture (Clemson HGIC's weekly-watering note, UMD's mulch-for-moisture note, and Missouri Botanical Garden's 'medium moisture' culture note), but none uses the phrase 'consistently moist' for this species, and the Clemson source explicitly frames watering as conditional ('if needed') rather than constant.

outdoor_sun_exposure omits part_sun and full_shade: no admissible source documents this species tolerating deep or dappled shade. NC State's structured Light field for Hydrangea paniculata lists only 'Full sun' and 'Partial Shade' as options -- notably different from NC State's own Hydrangea macrophylla page, which omits full sun entirely and instead lists Dappled Sunlight and Deep shade -- consistent with paniculata's documented greater sun tolerance relative to macrophylla.

UF/IFAS EDIS publication ENH457/ST298 ('Hydrangea paniculata: Panicle Hydrangea') is indexed in search results on edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ask.ifas.ufl.edu but returns HTTP 410 Gone on direct fetch of both https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/st298 and https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ST298 as of this research; its content could not be verified on the live page and so was not used as a citation source for any field.

Species-boundary check performed: all citations below were confirmed via direct page fetch to be on pages specifically titled/headed for Hydrangea paniculata (or an explicit 'Panicle hydrangea' subsection within a multi-species page, as on UMD's problems page), not reused Hydrangea macrophylla or genus-wide boilerplate. NC State's structured fields (Light, Soil Drainage, Problems) were confirmed distinct from its separate H. macrophylla page.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Live-fetch of the RHS source page confirms it lists 'Skin allergen: Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' as a distinct toxicity category, SEPARATE from 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten.' The skin-allergen/glove-handling instruction is RHS's human-handler safety caution, not a statement about animal toxicity. toxicity_detail merges the two into one sentence ('Skin allergen requiring gloves and other protective equipment when handling; harmful to dogs and cats if eaten') without flagging that the gloves/allergen clause is a human-only caution, not a pet-toxicity mechanism -- exactly the human-vs-animal content-boundary problem check 4 asks to guard against. The 'harmful to dogs and cats if eaten' portion is solid; the skin-allergen portion is not properly scoped to animals.

water_regime — removed on audit: The two citations labeled 'water_regime' are both weak. Live-fetch confirms the Clemson quote is 'Water them once a week, if needed, during the hottest and driest summer months' -- explicitly conditional ('if needed') and restricted to peak summer heat, which undercuts rather than supports a general 'keep_moist' (consistently-moist) characterization; the record's own unknowns text concedes this ('not a verbatim match... frames watering as conditional'). The UMD citation ('Mulch around the base of the plant to help to maintain moisture') is generic mulching advice, not a stated watering regime. The one citation whose quote text actually says 'medium moisture' (Missouri Botanical Garden, kempercode=c313) exists in the record but its claim label is 'outdoor_sun_exposure full_sun and part_shade,' not 'water_regime' -- so per the field-traceability rule it does not count as support for this field. No citation labeled for water_regime cleanly supports 'keep_moist.'

water_growing_days_est — removed on audit: The value 7 is drawn from the same Clemson quote ('once a week, if needed, during the hottest and driest summer months'), live-fetch-confirmed verbatim. That quote scopes the once-weekly figure explicitly to peak summer heat/drought and frames it as conditional, not a season-wide default. Applying it as the general 'water_growing_days_est' for the whole growing season extends the claim beyond what the source states -- the source gives no general growing-season watering interval, only a hottest/driest-month, if-needed figure.

water_estimate_basis — removed on audit: No citation's claim label contains 'water_estimate_basis,' so the field has no direct citation trace of its own under the record's stated rule. It also inherits the same over-extension problem flagged on water_regime/water_growing_days_est: it uses the Clemson 'hottest and driest summer months, if needed' figure to characterize a general water schedule, and while it partially discloses the conditionality, it still backs a season-wide numeric estimate with a source that only speaks to peak-heat conditions.

scientific_name_given: restored as "Hydrangea paniculata" -- this is the binomial the species was researched under (not a citation-derived claim), and this field is bookkeeping rather than a claim requiring citation traceability, matching every other record in this catalog. The audit's removal applied the citations-must-trace rule more strictly than the actual pipeline requires for this specific field.

records.toxicity_detail: Contains saponins as the toxic principle. RHS names dogs, cats, rabbits, and rodents as harmed if the plant is eaten. Clemson's pet-focused guidance (covering the corn plant specifically, distinct from other Dracaena species listed in the same article) describes symptoms of vomiting (sometimes bloody), depression, anorexia, and hypersalivation, with cats potentially showing dilated pupils.
records.cool_rest_note: Reduce watering from fall to late winter (growing-season watering should be uniformly moist, then cut back as temperatures cool).
records.water_dry_down_target: Allow soils to dry slightly between waterings, but never let them totally dry out.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max: NC State says corn plants "thrive in temperatures of 70 to 80 degrees F" while Missouri Botanical Garden says they are "best grown in temperatures of 60-75°F" — the two admissible species-specific sources disagree on the ideal daytime range, so left null rather than pick one.

night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives a species-specific night-temperature figure for D. fragrans (Clemson's day/night breakdown is generic Dracaena-genus care text, not fragrans-specific, so it was excluded).

humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/humidity_need: no admissible source gives a specific percentage or qualitative humidity label for D. fragrans itself; Clemson's genus-wide Dracaena factsheet gives a '30 to 40 percent' figure but it is not specific to this species, so it was not used.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives foot-candle figures or a stated hours-of-direct-sun number for this species; NC State's Dappled Sunlight/Deep shade/Partial Shade entries are generic, site-wide light-category labels rather than a species-specific hours figure.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: RHS lists pH tolerance only as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (i.e. broadly tolerant of all categories), not a numeric range.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength/fertilize_interval_days: RHS says to 'apply a balanced liquid feed monthly' during the growing season but never names specific calendar months or a feed strength/dilution, and translating 'monthly' into a numeric day-interval (e.g. 30) would go beyond what the quote literally states, so all three were left null.

water_regime keep_moist relies on NC State's and Missouri Botanical Garden's species-specific culture text (both instruct keeping the soil moist during the growing season); Clemson's Dracaena factsheet also contains drier-sounding watering advice ('allow to dry slightly... wait until the soil surface is dry to the touch') but that text is generic Dracaena-genus care rather than fragrans-specific, so it was not treated as a competing citation and the field was not nulled.

toxicity_detail deliberately avoids NC State's own 'Poison Symptoms' text (which happens to name cats and dogs) because that text sits inside a field group whose header literally reads 'Poisonous to Humans:' on the source page; NC State's separate, non-human-headed 'Problem for Cats'/'Problem for Dogs' tags were used instead to support toxic_to_pets, and toxicity_detail draws on Clemson's pets-focused article and RHS instead.

outdoor_sun_exposure includes full_sun from RHS's structured Position field, though NC State's and Clemson's indoor-culture prose both warn that direct/too much sun can burn foliage or prevent best leaf color indoors; treated as addressing different contexts (outdoor/greenhouse position vs. indoor placement) rather than a direct conflict, but noted here for transparency.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The 'full_sun' entry rests solely on RHS's structured Position tag ('Full sun, Partial shade'). Verified against the live pages, three independent pieces of species-specific evidence point the other way: NC State's own structured Light field for Dracaena fragrans lists only 'Dappled Sunlight', 'Deep shade', and 'Partial Shade' (Full Sun is not an option checked), plus its prose says 'Direct sun can burn the foliage.' MOBOT's structured Sun field is 'Part shade' only, with prose warning the plant should be 'protected from significant periods of direct sun' and that 'too much sun may prevent best foliage color from developing.' Even RHS's own cultivation prose (same source as the Position tag) hedges with 'Grow in peat-free, loam-based potting compost in full light with shade from hot sun' -- undercutting its own structured tag. The unknowns note rationalizes this as 'different contexts (outdoor/greenhouse position vs. indoor placement)' but nothing in any source ties the Position tag or RHS's cultivation advice specifically to outdoor-only siting, so this is a real, undisclosed-in-full disagreement resolved by picking the minority-supported value. 'part_shade' is not in question -- only 'full_sun' is unsound.

records.name_note: NC State Extension lists Cornus kousa's former synonyms as "Benthamia japonica, Benthamia kousa, Benthamidia japonica, Cynoxylon kousa, Dendrobenthamia japonica," and RHS's Synonyms field lists an overlapping but not identical set: "Benthamia japonica, Benthamidia japonica, Benthamidia kousa, Cornus japonica, Dendrobenthamia japonica." Both admissible sources that address name status treat Cornus kousa itself as the current, correct name -- RHS's own structured Name Status field reads "Correct" -- unlike the sibling species Cornus florida already in this catalog, where Penn State Extension's taxonomy article argues the accepted name is now Benthamidia florida. That same Penn State article was checked directly for this record and does not name Cornus kousa or Benthamidia kousa anywhere, so no admissible source disputes Cornus kousa as the accepted name for this species.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max/cool_rest_note: these read as indoor-microclimate and container-culture fields; no admissible source discusses ambient indoor temperature, humidity, foot-candle light levels, or a direct-sun-hour ceiling for this outdoor landscape tree/shrub.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives an actionable cold-damage-onset temperature. Sources give only USDA hardiness-zone survival ranges: NC State Extension lists zones 5a-8b, UF/IFAS lists 5B through 8B, UGA CAES gives Georgia's hardy zones as 6b and 7, and RHS rates it H6 ('hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)' degrees C). None of these describe the temperature at which damage begins, only the zone in which the plant is expected to survive winters, so this was left null.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: no admissible source addresses toxicity to pets (or humans) for Cornus kousa. NC State Extension's tag set -- which for many other species in this catalog carries explicit toxic/non-toxic tags -- carries no toxicity tags of any kind on this species' page (confirmed by inspecting the full attribute and tag list). RHS's plant profile page has no Pets or Poisonous section at all (confirmed directly by searching the fetched page: the words 'toxic', 'poison', 'pets', 'cats', 'dogs', and 'horses' do not appear anywhere on it). Clemson's and UF/IFAS's dedicated Kousa dogwood/dogwood factsheets discuss only the fruit's edibility to humans and birds, never toxicity. Left null per this catalog's rule against inferring toxicity from genus or family.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State's only pH datapoint for this species is the site-wide categorical tag 'Soil pH: Acid (<6.0)' -- this catalog has already confirmed elsewhere (e.g. the Acer rubrum record) that this exact bucket string is generic, reused site-wide boilerplate rather than a species-curated number, so it was not used here either. RHS's structured pH field is even less specific -- 'pH: Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' spans essentially the entire scale. Clemson and UF/IFAS describe the soil only qualitatively as 'acidic', with no literal number given anywhere for this species. Both fields left null.

water_regime (flagged because this field is treated as harm-capable): admissible sources genuinely disagree on how drought-tolerant this species is, and one source disagrees with itself. University of Maryland Extension states Kousa dogwood 'has a longer and later bloom season than the native flowering dogwood (Cornus florida), plus different growth characteristics and a greater tolerance for dry conditions' -- i.e. more drought-tolerant than the already moisture-loving native. Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC's dogwood factsheet states close to the opposite: the species 'does not tolerate drought, and should be deeply irrigated during hot, dry spells.' UF/IFAS's own publication contradicts itself on this exact point: its structured field reads 'Drought tolerance: moderate,' while its own prose two paragraphs later reads 'Kousa dogwood is not particularly drought- or heat-tolerant, requiring irrigation during drought periods in summer.' NC State Extension takes a middle position -- 'while it tolerates some dry soil, it will not survive in waterlogged environments' -- and Missouri Botanical Garden rates water need merely 'Medium' while also noting the plant 'Appreciates regular moisture during hot summers.' Given this spread, and the direct internal conflict within the UF/IFAS source, water_regime was left null rather than picking a side.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis/water_dry_down_target: no admissible source frames watering as a checkable numeric schedule (soil-probe depth, day intervals) for this in-ground landscape tree; the drought/irrigation guidance that does exist (Clemson's 'should be deeply irrigated during hot, dry spells,' UF/IFAS's 'requiring irrigation during drought periods in summer') is qualitative only, with no numbers to anchor an estimate, and is itself part of the water_regime conflict noted above.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a specific fertilizing schedule, calendar month, or dilution guidance for Cornus kousa. UF/IFAS's only fertilizing mention is generic borer-prevention advice -- 'Try to keep the trees healthy with regular fertilization' -- with no month, interval, or strength specified.

scientific_name_accepted / name_note: confirmed as Cornus kousa without conflict. The sibling species already in this catalog, Cornus florida, has scientific_name_accepted left null because Penn State Extension's taxonomy article argues the currently accepted name is now Benthamidia florida. That same Penn State article was checked directly for this record and does not name Cornus kousa or Benthamidia kousa anywhere -- only Cornus florida/Benthamidia florida and Cornus alternifolia are named. Both admissible sources that give a name-status determination for Cornus kousa specifically (RHS's structured 'Name Status: Correct' field, and NC State's 'Previously known as' list, which places Benthamidia kousa only among former synonyms) agree Cornus kousa is current, so no null was needed here.

NC State Extension's and RHS's synonym lists for Cornus kousa overlap but are not identical -- NC State's 'Previously known as' list includes Cynoxylon kousa (which RHS's Synonyms list omits), and RHS's list includes Cornus japonica (which NC State's list omits). This is a difference in list completeness between the two sources, not a disagreement about which name is currently accepted, so it does not affect scientific_name_accepted.

records.name_note: RHS's Name Status field reads "Correct" for Zingiber officinale with no conflicting accepted name found on any admissible source, so there is no naming conflict to flag.
records.cool_rest_note: Penn State Extension: ginger goes dormant and loses its stems with the onset of winter; the rhizomes can be left in their container with soil over winter, or dug up, cleaned, and stored in a brown paper bag in a cool, dry place until spring (do not refrigerate rhizomes intended for replanting).
records.water_dry_down_target: Water sparingly right after planting, until the plant starts to grow / top growth develops (to avoid rhizome rot in cold, wet soil); once established, keep soil evenly moist but not soggy, watering (and fertilizing) regularly to heavily. NC State: "To avoid root rot water sparingly until the plant starts to grow, then water and fertilize regularly." Missouri Botanical Garden: "Water sparingly until top growth develops, otherwise the rhizome could rot. Once established, water heavily, fertilize monthly, and keep in a partially shaded location."
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: left null. No admissible source addresses toxicity to pets (or humans) for this species. NC State's Tags line for Zingiber officinale carries no toxicity-related tag at all ('#edible roots #annual herb #heat tolerant #humidity tolerant #herbaceous #tropical #tropical herbaceous perennial #herbaceous perennial #edible spice #vhfn-h #vhfn #frost tender #annual #edible'), and the RHS plant profile page has no Poisonous to Humans / Poisonous to Pets section at all for this species.

day_f_min, day_f_max, and night_f_max: left null. Only a night-temperature floor was found (Penn State Extension: 'make sure night temperatures do not go below 50 degrees,' captured in night_f_min) and a general cold-protection threshold (captured in chill_damage_f, corroborated by NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden both independently naming 50°F as the point to bring the plant indoors). No admissible source splits out a full daytime range or a night ceiling.

light_fc_min and light_fc_good: left null. No admissible source gives a foot-candle figure for this species; light guidance only comes in hours of direct sun (captured in direct_sun_hours_max) or category terms (Partial Shade / Part shade).
humidity_pct_min and humidity_pct_max: left null. Sources describe humidity only qualitatively ('high humidity,' 'hot, humid conditions,' 'humidity tolerant'); none gives a percentage figure.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, and fertilize_strength: left null. Missouri Botanical Garden says to 'fertilize monthly' once established, but 'monthly' is a frequency word, not a literal day-interval number, so per the numeric-literal-match rule it cannot support fertilize_interval_days (30 does not appear in the quote). Penn State names a '5-5-5 fertilizer mixture' (an NPK ratio), which is fertilizer composition, not a full/half/quarter dilution strength, so it does not map to fertilize_strength. No admissible source names specific calendar months.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis: left null. No admissible source gives a specific check-depth or day-interval watering figure for this species; only qualitative moisture guidance was found, captured instead in water_regime and water_dry_down_target.

direct_sun_hours_max: set to 5, sourced from the NC State Zingiber genus page's own descriptive prose ('2 to 5 hours of direct sunlight') and Penn State's '2 - 5 hours of direct daily sunlight,' rather than from the Zingiber officinale species page's structured 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' tag. That structured tag is NC State's sitewide standard definition of the 'Partial Shade' category (the identical 2-6 hour wording is boilerplate used across many unrelated species pages, not officinale-specific measured guidance), so the narrower, cultivation-specific '2 to 5 hours' figure was preferred instead. Note also that the NC State genus page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/zingiber/) formally covers the ~140-species Zingiber genus rather than officinale alone, but its growing-guide prose (the 50°F cold threshold, rot risk in cold/wet soil, container culture) closely parallels the officinale species page and is illustrated with Z. officinale photos, so it was treated as applicable here while being flagged for transparency.

outdoor_sun_exposure: set to ['part_shade'] only, not full_sun. RHS's own structured Position field lists 'Full sun, Partial shade' as options, but RHS's own cultivation prose recommends 'filtered sunlight' (not full unfiltered sun), and NC State's officinale-specific prose explicitly warns 'Placing plants in full sun can result in the foliage tipped with brown and poor growth.' Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Sun field is 'Part shade' and Clemson recommends 'a location with afternoon shade.' Given this weight of evidence against full sun, full_sun was not included despite appearing in RHS's Position checkbox.

soil_drainage: set to moderate on the balance of the evidence, despite mild tension with NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species ('Moist,' 'Occasionally Wet' -- notably not 'Good Drainage'). RHS's structured Moisture field literally reads 'Moist but well–drained,' and Clemson's prose independently says 'evenly moist, but not soggy,' both pointing the same direction; NC State's own prose also warns 'Cold and/or wet locations can cause root rot,' which is consistent with wanting some drainage rather than standing water. moderate was chosen as the value that best matches 'moist but well-drained' without forcing 'fast' or 'moisture_retentive.'

soil_base: set to standard_potting from Penn State's container-growing passage ('loamy, rich organic soil') rather than a more specific enum, since no source names an actual potting-mix product; this is the closest fit to a general enriched container mix, not a specialty mix like cactus_succulent or orchid_bark.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State's own pH tags for this species ('Acid <6.0, Alkaline >8.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0') cover almost the entire scale and were treated as non-specific boilerplate category coverage, not a real preference range; the specific 5.5-6.5 figure came only from Penn State Extension.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The only citation supporting this field (claim: 'scientific_name_accepted Zingiber officinale (Name Status Correct)') has a quote that is almost entirely RHS's generic Genus-level description box ('Genus Zingiber are aromatic rhizomatous perennials with alternate, oblong leaves in two ranks, and cone-like inflorescences...') -- boilerplate that RHS shows on every species page within the ~140-species Zingiber genus, not officinale-specific content. The words 'Name Status Correct' are tacked onto the end with no connecting punctuation and no explicit subject; the quote never actually contains the string 'officinale' or otherwise ties the 'Correct' status to this specific binomial. Per the re-derivation standard (does the quote literally state the value?), this citation does not literally establish that 'Zingiber officinale' itself carries a confirmed/correct name status -- it establishes generic genus traits plus an unattributed status word. There is no second, independent citation for this field to fall back on, so the field's only support is this weak/ambiguous one, meaning the value itself (not just one citation among several) is in doubt.

records.name_note: RHS's own database confirms Armoracia rusticana as the correct current name for this species (Name Status: Correct) while separately flagging two historical/synonymous names for the same plant as Synonym: Brassica amoracia 'Rusticana' and Cochlearia armoracia. NC State Extension corroborates, listing Cochlearia armoracia under "Previously known as" for this species. No admissible source disputes Armoracia rusticana as the accepted binomial, so there is no naming conflict to record.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: no admissible source addresses pet toxicity for horseradish. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page for this species (which does carry Poisonous-to-Humans/Poisonous-to-Pets sections for many other species) has neither section for Armoracia rusticana, and RHS's species page likewise has no Pets/toxicity block. No usable UF/IFAS, Clemson, Penn State, or UGA page was found either (see below).

day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: no admissible source gives an ambient growing-temperature range for the living plant. The only Fahrenheit figures found for this species (University of Maryland Extension's Mid-Atlantic commercial production guide: 'Store horseradish in the dark with temperatures between 32-40°F (0-4°C) and 98% relative humidity') describe post-harvest cold storage of the dug root, not the growing plant's ambient temperature, so it was not mapped here.

chill_damage_f: RHS gives only a winter-survival hardiness rating (H6: 'hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)' °C), which is a survival floor rather than the actionable damage-onset temperature this field calls for; no admissible source gives a damage-onset figure.

cool_rest_note: RHS's grow-your-own guide states the plant 'goes dormant over winter, the leaves dying down in autumn then re-sprouting from the roots every spring,' but this is ordinary outdoor perennial dormancy with no actionable rest-period instruction (no target temperature, no watering-reduction step, no move-to-cooler-spot direction), so it was not used for this field.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source, consistent with this not being grown as an indoor plant.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives a foot-candle light measurement for this species.
direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day' defines the minimum threshold for its 'Full sun' category, not a maximum for this species.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: NC State tags all three of its pH bands for this species (Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, Alkaline >8.0) and RHS states pH tolerance only as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- both are effectively unrestricted rather than a bounded range, so no numeric min/max was set.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: RHS's grow-your-own guide splits watering practice by setting -- container plants are kept 'evenly moist' during the growing season, especially in warm weather, while ground-planted horseradish needs water only during dry spells in its first year and needs no additional watering once established. This setting-dependent, non-scheduled practice doesn't map cleanly onto a check-depth or fixed day-count interval, and no admissible source gives either directly.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: RHS's grow-your-own guide gives a specific fertilizing schedule (liquid feed 'applied every few weeks from mid-spring to late summer') only for container-grown plants, while explicitly stating 'Horseradish grown in the ground shouldn't need any additional feeding.' Since soil_base is recorded as garden_bed (the setting every admissible source treats as the default for this vegetable-garden crop), applying the container-only schedule here would misrepresent it as general guidance, so all three fields were left null.

soil_base: RHS's grow-your-own consumer guide actually recommends against open-ground planting ('Planting horseradish in open ground isn't recommended, as it forms a vigorous spreading clump that can be hard to control or remove') and favors container culture instead, while still acknowledging ground planting is workable ('If you're happy for horseradish to spread, you can plant it in the ground.'). This is a real venue-preference difference from NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden (both describe garden-bed vegetable-garden cultivation as the norm) and from RHS's own species page (which gives straightforward in-ground cultivation instructions with no container caveat). garden_bed was recorded as the majority/default value; the RHS grow-guide's contrary container recommendation is flagged here rather than silently dropped.

UF/IFAS: the only UF/IFAS publication specific to horseradish, EDIS HS611/MV078 ('Horseradish--Armoracia rusticana Gaertn., Mey., Scherb.'), has been retired from the site -- both https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/mv078 and https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/mv078 return HTTP 410 Gone on direct fetch as of this research -- so despite search-engine result snippets still summarizing its old content (e.g., that horseradish 'does not grow well in Florida'), it could not be used as a live, quotable admissible source. No other UF/IFAS page found gives horseradish cultivation guidance; the only other hits name horseradish merely as a host plant for unrelated pests (nematodes, harlequin bug, tarnished plant bug).

Clemson Cooperative Extension (hgic.clemson.edu), Penn State Extension (extension.psu.edu), and UGA Cooperative Extension (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu) were all searched but no dedicated horseradish factsheet, care guide, or pet-toxicity/vegetable-chart entry naming horseradish was found on any of the three sites as of this research; a Penn State URL titled 'Growing Horseradish' found via search now 301-redirects to an unrelated generic home-gardening page with no horseradish content.

soil_base — removed on audit: Genuine, unresolved disagreement among admissible sources on this consequential field: RHS's Grow Your Own guide (confirmed live) explicitly says 'Planting horseradish in open ground isn't recommended, as it forms a vigorous spreading clump that can be hard to control or remove' and recommends container culture instead, while NC State (x2) and Missouri Botanical Garden support garden_bed. None of the three citations backing garden_bed is itself defective or mis-quoted (all verified accurate live) -- the dissenting RHS source is an equally admissible, differently-reasoned recommendation, not a bad citation to discount. The record candidly discloses this conflict in unknowns but still resolves it by picking garden_bed as a 'majority/default' rather than leaving the field null, which is the over-reach check 2 targets: a real cross-source disagreement on a field whose wrong value steers users toward a stated hard-to-reverse consequence.

records.name_note: RHS's Liatris spicata plant profile lists "Name Status: Correct" for this binomial, and no admissible source (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, Penn State Extension, or the others searched) proposes a different accepted name or flags a synonym conflict, so scientific_name_accepted is set to the given name with no ambiguity to record.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: none of the admissible sources searched (NC State Extension, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS EDIS/Ask IFAS, RHS, Penn State Extension, UMD Extension, UGA CAES) discuss toxicity of Liatris spicata to cats, dogs, or humans at all; left null rather than inferring from general Asteraceae/genus knowledge.

chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note: no admissible source states an actionable cold-damage-onset temperature. Only general USDA hardiness-zone ranges turned up, and those disagree by source (NC State/Missouri Botanical Garden ~zones 3-8; RHS Hardiness rating H7, i.e. 'hardy in the severest European continental climates (< -20C)'; Penn State's 'dense-blazing-star' page says zones 5-10 while Penn State's 'rain-garden' page says zones 3-9) -- none of these is a damage-onset figure and there's no schema field for hardiness zone, so chill_damage_f stays null.
day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max: no admissible source gives specific daytime or nighttime temperature comfort ranges for this outdoor perennial; left null.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity or foot-candle light levels -- these are outdoor-garden sources describing sun exposure only in categorical terms (full sun / partial shade), not indoor/container light metrics; left null.
fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a fertilizer schedule or feeding strength for Liatris spicata; left null.

water_regime and the other water_* fields (water_check_depth_cm, water_dormant_days_est, water_dry_down_target, water_estimate_basis, water_growing_days_est): sources describe general outdoor watering as 'Water: Medium' (Missouri Botanical Garden) with the plant tolerating drought once established while preferring 'moist, fertile' soil and being 'Intolerant of wet soils in winter' (Missouri Botanical Garden), and Penn State similarly says it 'prefers moisture but can also tolerate some drought.' None of this maps cleanly onto the catalog's houseplant-style watering enum (keep_moist / dry_surface_between / dry_thoroughly_between / keep_barely_moist), so these fields were left null rather than force-fit into a container-watering vocabulary that doesn't describe an in-ground garden perennial.
soil_ph_min: only an upper bound was found ('<6.8', Penn State Extension, corroborated on two Penn State pages); no admissible source states a specific lower pH bound, so soil_ph_min is left null.

soil_ph_max resolution: NC State's Plant Toolbox selects both 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' as Soil pH categories for this species -- a coarse, site-wide checkbox categorization whose combined range extends up to pH 8.0 -- while Penn State Extension gives a specific preferred figure of pH <6.8 on two separate pages. Because NC State's field is a bucketed category rather than a precise number, I used Penn State's specific figure (6.8) for soil_ph_max rather than blending it with NC State's broader category ceiling of 8.0; NC State's coarser tolerance range is noted here rather than folded into the numeric field.

is_houseplant: no admissible source describes growing Liatris spicata indoors or in containers long-term; every source (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, Penn State) describes it strictly as an outdoor garden/meadow/prairie perennial, so is_houseplant is set to false on that consistent absence rather than any single explicit 'not a houseplant' statement.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: The value 6.8 rests on two citations that are NOT independent corroboration — both are Penn State Extension pages ('extension.psu.edu/dense-blazing-star' and 'extension.psu.edu/rain-garden-plants-blazing-star-liatris-spicata'), and one of them is phrased as a personal aside ('The pH value I found that Liatris prefers is <6.8...') rather than an institutional fact-sheet statement. Meanwhile NC State's Plant Toolbox — a separate, admissible, and elsewhere-cited authoritative source — selects BOTH 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' as tolerated soil-pH categories for this species (per the record's own unknowns note), i.e. it documents tolerance up to pH 8.0, directly conflicting with capping soil_ph_max at 6.8. The record's unknowns section acknowledges this conflict but resolves it by simply preferring the single-institution Penn State figure over NC State's broader range rather than nulling the field — this is exactly the 'sources disagree and the record picked one value anyway' defect, and unlike outdoor_sun_exposure there is no truly independent second source to save the field under the check-2 carve-out. Separately, both Penn State quotes state the bound as a strict '<6.8' (less than), while the field records an inclusive max of exactly 6.8 — a minor but real mismatch between the quoted inequality and the stored number.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The sole supporting citation's quote is a concatenated scrape of unrelated RHS page sections ('Habit Tufted Genus Liatris are herbaceous perennials with narrow, grass-like foliage and erect, bottlebrush-like spikes of flowers which open from the top down Name Status Correct Plant Range E North America') and never actually contains the string 'Liatris spicata' anywhere in the quoted text. The tie between 'Name Status: Correct' and the specific epithet 'spicata' is inferred only from the page URL slug ('liatris-spicata-button-snakewort-dense-blazing-star'), not from anything stated in the quote itself — re-deriving the value strictly from the quote text (as instructed), a strict reading cannot rule out that 'Name Status: Correct' refers to the genus description or another name on the page rather than specifically confirming the binomial 'Liatris spicata.' This is the only citation supporting the field (no independent backup), so under the 'default to refuted=true when unsure' instruction this thin, context-dependent (URL-only) linkage is flagged, even though the real-world fact is very likely correct and no source contradicts it.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: fifteenth batch of the "blind spots" pass. Belladonna (deadly nightshade) is one of history's most infamous toxic plants -- confirmed toxic_to_pets=true with clean, explicit cat and dog evidence from all three admissible sources, and correctly left scientific_name_accepted null on a genuine spelling split (NC State: "Atropa bella-donna", hyphenated; RHS and MOBOT: unhyphenated) that neither source acknowledges or resolves. Bittersweet Nightshade also confirmed toxic_to_pets=true, both properly checked against this batch's non-cat/dog toxicity-scope guard with no defects found this round. Rounded out with Panicle Hydrangea (a deliberate companion to Bigleaf Hydrangea, already in this catalog, with notably different sun tolerance), Corn Plant, Kousa Dogwood (a clean pass, 0 fields removed), Ginger, Horseradish, and Blazing Star.

One landing-time repair: Panicle Hydrangea's scientific_name_given was nulled by the audit for lacking its own dedicated citation, but that field is bookkeeping (the binomial the species was researched under), not a claim requiring citation traceability under the actual pipeline rules -- restored directly rather than left null, which would have been inconsistent with every other record in this catalog.

Ginger and Blazing Star both landed scientific_name_accepted null on citation-quality grounds worth noting as a pattern: both citations were RHS genus-level description boxes with a bare "Name Status Correct" tag stapled on with no text actually tying that status to the specific species epithet -- the audit correctly refused to accept a page-URL-only inference ("the URL slug says spicata, so this must be about spicata") as sufficient under the literal re-derivation standard, even though the underlying facts are very likely correct.

Horseradish's soil_base landed null after the audit found a genuine, undissolved disagreement it hadn't fully credited: RHS's own growing guide explicitly recommends AGAINST open-ground planting ("forms a vigorous spreading clump that can be hard to control or remove") and recommends containers instead, while NC State and MOBOT support garden-bed planting -- a real conflict with a stated hard-to-reverse consequence for whichever way a reader goes, not a case where one source is simply wrong.
